questions.title: Carcinoma in situ has not yet invaded the basement membrane
questions.question: An epithelial neoplasm exhibiting all the cellular features associated with malignancy, but which has not yet invaded through the epithelial basement membrane is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carcinosarcoma is a distinct, mixed malignant tumour containing both carcinomatous and sarcomatous elements, not the pre-invasive lesion this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This option is simply a misspelling of carcinoma in situ, not a different named entity; the correctly spelled option is the one the printed key marks.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anaplastic describes a degree of poor cellular differentiation, not the specific pre-invasive-versus-invasive distinction this stem is testing.
explanations.D: Correct. Carcinoma in situ (CIS) represents a pre-invasive stage of carcinoma, showing full-thickness epithelial atypia (severe dysplasia) with all the cytological features of malignancy, but without invasion of the basement membrane. The basement membrane, not cytological appearance, is the feature that separates CIS from an actual invasive carcinoma, and once it is breached the CIS phase ends and a truly invasive malignant tumour begins.

questions.title: Basal cell carcinoma is one of the locally malignant tumours
questions.question: One of the locally malignant tumours is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Liposarcoma is a frankly malignant mesenchymal tumour of fat, not one of the department book's named intermediate/locally malignant tumours.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma is a frankly malignant epithelial tumour with genuine metastatic potential, not a locally malignant one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is a frankly malignant bone tumour, not one of the intermediate/locally malignant category.
explanations.D: Correct. Basal cell carcinoma is one of the department book's named intermediate (locally malignant) tumours, alongside giant cell tumour of bone (osteoclastoma), adamantinoma, carcinoid tumour, chordoma and craniopharyngioma. These tumours are locally invasive and destructive and can recur after excision. They rarely metastasise, though, and so carry a better prognosis than frankly malignant tumours.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chondrosarcoma is a frankly malignant cartilage tumour, not one of the intermediate/locally malignant category.

questions.title: Osteoclastoma is a locally malignant tumour
questions.question: Osteoclastoma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Osteoclastoma is locally invasive and destructive, more than a purely benign tumour, so it is not classified as simply benign.
explanations.B: Correct. Osteoclastoma (giant cell tumour of bone) is one of the department book's named intermediate (locally malignant) tumours, alongside basal cell carcinoma, adamantinoma, carcinoid tumour, chordoma and craniopharyngioma. It is locally invasive and destructive and is prone to recurrence after curettage. It rarely metastasises, though, and so carries a better prognosis than a frankly malignant tumour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteoclastoma is not itself a metastatic deposit from elsewhere; the term describes a primary bone tumour of this specific behavioural category.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteoclastoma does not behave as a frankly (fully) malignant tumour, since it rarely metastasises, unlike osteosarcoma.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteoclastoma is a true neoplasm, not a tumour-like (non-neoplastic) condition.

questions.title: The spleen is not among the commonly affected metastatic sites
questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true about distant metastases:

options.A: Lungs and liver are common sites for metastases.
options.B: Histology of metastatic tumors usually resembles that of the primary tumor.
options.C: Omental metastases are commonly accompanied by hemorrhagic ascites
options.D: Skeletal muscles and intestine are rarely affected by metastases.
options.E: Spleen is among the most commonly affected sites.

explanations.A: Incorrect (as the false statement) -- this statement is true. The liver and lungs are among the department book's named common sites of haematogenous metastasis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (as the false statement) -- this statement is true. A metastatic tumour's histology usually resembles its primary site of origin, which is how pathologists trace an unknown metastasis back to its source.
explanations.C: Incorrect (as the false statement) -- this statement is true. Omental metastases commonly produce haemorrhagic ascites in the department's teaching.
explanations.D: Incorrect (as the false statement) -- this statement is true. Skeletal muscle and intestine are explicitly listed as rare sites of metastasis, despite being richly vascular.
explanations.E: Correct (as the false statement). The department book grosses the common sites of haematogenous metastasis as liver, lungs, bone and brain, explicitly listing muscle, spleen, pancreas and intestine as RARE sites instead. So "spleen is among the most commonly affected sites" is the one statement here that is not true, despite the spleen's own rich blood supply.

questions.title: Carcinoma in situ is an intraepithelial carcinoma
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true for carcinoma in situ:

options.A: it is mild degree of dysplasia.
options.B: It predisposes to the development of fibrosarcoma.
options.C: It is characterized by cellular atypia accompanied by basement membrane invasion.
options.E: It may appear grossly as an irregular ulcer with everted edges.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carcinoma in situ shows severe, not mild, epithelial dysplasia -- full-thickness cellular atypia with disturbed polarity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carcinoma in situ, if untreated, progresses to invasive carcinoma of the same epithelial lineage, not to fibrosarcoma, a mesenchymal tumour of an entirely different lineage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carcinoma in situ is defined precisely by cellular atypia WITHOUT basement membrane invasion; invasion of the basement membrane is what ends the CIS phase and marks the start of truly invasive carcinoma.
explanations.D: Correct. Carcinoma in situ is an intraepithelial carcinoma: full-thickness epithelial atypia with all the cytological features of malignancy, confined entirely within the epithelium and its intact basement membrane. This intraepithelial confinement, not a mild degree of dysplasia, a predisposition to fibrosarcoma, or a grossly ulcerated appearance, is what defines it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An irregular ulcer with everted edges describes the gross appearance of an invasive malignant ulcer, not the microscopic, pre-invasive entity carcinoma in situ.
